subject: maths
title: Integers, decimals and rounding

slides.heading: What are integers — and why does rounding matter?
slides.body: Integers are all whole numbers: ..., −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, ... — no decimals, no fractions. Every real measurement is rounded, because no ruler or stopwatch is perfectly precise. Knowing how to round correctly means your answers match what the question actually asks for.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: The rounding rule — decimal places and significant figures
slides.body: Find the digit immediately to the right of where you are rounding. If that digit is 5 or more, round the target digit up by 1; if it is 4 or less, leave it unchanged and drop everything after. This same rule applies whether you are rounding to decimal places (d.p.) or significant figures (s.f.).
slides.note: Second concept slide used here because rounding has no single algebraic formula — it is a decision rule.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: Round 5.3864 to (a) 2 decimal places and (b) 2 significant figures.

steps.instruction: Look at the 3rd decimal place (the deciding digit) to round to 2 d.p.
steps.working: The 3rd d.p. digit is 6. Since 6 ≥ 5, round up: 8 becomes 9.

steps.instruction: For 2 significant figures, count from the first non-zero digit.
steps.working: 5 is the 1st s.f., 3 is the 2nd s.f. The deciding digit is 8. Since 8 ≥ 5, round up: 3 becomes 4.

slides.conclusion: 5.3864 rounded to 2 d.p. = 5.39; rounded to 2 s.f. = 5.4.
slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Looking at the digit in the rounding position rather than the one to its right — e.g. rounding 3.8512 to 2 d.p., the student sees 5 in the 2nd d.p. position and rounds up the 8, giving 3.86, when the deciding digit is actually 1 (the 3rd d.p.) and the answer is 3.85.
mistakes.correction: Always look one place to the right of where you are rounding — that is the deciding digit.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing decimal places and significant figures — writing 5.39 when asked for 2 s.f. (answer should be 5.4) or writing 5.4 when asked for 2 d.p. (answer should be 5.39).
mistakes.correction: Decimal places count digits after the decimal point. Significant figures count digits from the first non-zero digit, including those before the decimal point.

mistakes.mistake: Not carrying a round-up through all digits — e.g. rounding 6.96 to 1 d.p. and writing 6.9 because the student does not recognise that 9 rounds up to 10, which changes the units digit.
mistakes.correction: Carry the round-up as far as it goes: 6.96 → 7.0 to 1 d.p.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: Integers are whole numbers: ..., −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, ... Decimals and fractions are not integers.
keyFacts.examTip: If a question asks for an integer solution, check your answer is a whole number — not a decimal.

keyFacts.fact: To round to n decimal places, look at the (n+1)th decimal digit. If it is 5 or more, round up; if 4 or less, round down.
keyFacts.examTip: Circle the deciding digit in your working to avoid using the wrong one.

keyFacts.fact: Significant figures are counted from the first non-zero digit. Leading zeros (e.g. in 0.0047) are not significant.
keyFacts.examTip: 0.0047 to 1 s.f. is 0.005, not 0.0 — the first significant figure is 4.

keyFacts.fact: 6.96 rounded to 1 d.p. is 7.0 — write 7.0, not just 7, to show the answer is given to 1 decimal place.
keyFacts.examTip: Trailing zeros after the decimal point are significant and must be included when rounding is specified.

note: keyFacts: 2-4 entries. Exam-precise language. These are what Mabel writes into her notes.
